title: De Ira Dei
author: Lactantius
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0171.stoa006.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's CSEL and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: si ergo nulla est sapientia humana, ut Socrates docuit, ut Plato tradidit, apparet esse diuinam nec ulli alii quam deo ueritatis notitiam subiacere.
passages.english: If, then, there is no human wisdom, as Socrates taught and as Plato handed down, it is evident that [wisdom] is divine, and that knowledge of the truth lies within the reach of no one other than God.

passages.original: denique Marcus Tullius a Posidonio dictum refert id Epicurum sensisse, nullos deos esse, sed ea quae de dis locutus sit depellendae inuidiae causa dixisse: itaque uerbis illum deos relinquere, re autem ipsa tollere, quibus nullum motum, nullum tribuit officium.
passages.english: Indeed, Marcus Tullius reports that Posidonius said that Epicurus held this view, that there are no gods, but that what he said about the gods he said for the sake of warding off ill will; and so in words he leaves the gods in place, but in actual fact does away with them, since he assigns them no movement and no function.

passages.original: propterea nullum est animal, ut ait Cicero, praeter hominem quod habeat notitiam aliquam dei. solus enim sapientia instructus est, ut religionem solus intellegat, et haec est hominis atque mutorum uel praecipua uel sola distantia.
passages.english: For this reason there is no animal, as Cicero says, except man, that has any knowledge of God. For he alone has been furnished with wisdom, so that he alone may understand religion, and this is either the chief or the only difference between man and the dumb animals.

passages.original: at enim naturam excellentem honorari oportet. quis honos deberi potest nihil curanti et ingrato ? an aliqua ratione obstricti esse possumus ei qui nihil habeat commune nobiscum? deus inquit Cicero si talis est ut nulla gratia, nulla hominum caritate teneatur, ualeat. quid enim dicam \'propitius sit\'? esse enim propitius potest nemini. quid contemptius dici potuit in deum?
passages.english: But, [they say], a surpassing nature ought to be honoured. What honour can be owed to one who cares for nothing and is ungrateful? Or can we be bound by any obligation to one who has nothing in common with us? "If God," says Cicero, "is such that he is held by no favour, by no love for men, farewell to him. For why should I say 'may he be propitious'? For he can be propitious to no one." What more contemptuous thing could be said against God?

passages.original: haec dum sentit Epicurus, religionem funditus delet: qua sublata confusio ac perturbatio uitae sequetur.
passages.english: While Epicurus holds these views, he destroys religion from its foundations; and when it is taken away, confusion and disorder of life will follow.

passages.original: postea uero Epicurus deum quidem esse dixit, quia necesse sit esse aliquid in mundo praestans et eximium et beatum, prouidentiam tamen nullam: itaque mundum ipsum nec ratione ulla nec arte nec fabrica instructum, sed naturam rerum quibusdam minutis seminibus et insecabilibus conglobatam.
passages.english: Later, however, Epicurus said that there is indeed a god, because there must necessarily be something in the world that is pre-eminent, exceptional and blessed, yet [that there is] no providence; and so [he said] that the world itself was not constructed by any reason or art or workmanship, but that the nature of things was massed together from certain tiny and indivisible seeds.

passages.original: nonne prodigio simile est aut natum esse hominem qui haec diceret aut extitisse qui crederent, ut Democritum, qui auditor eius fuit, uel Epicurum, in quem uanitas omnis de Leucippi fonte profluxit ?
passages.english: Is it not like a portent either that a man was born who would say these things, or that there arose men who would believe them, such as Democritus, who was his pupil, or Epicurus, into whom all the folly flowed from the spring of Leucippus?

passages.original: si quid est inquit Chrysippus quod efficiat ea quae homo, licet ratione sit praeditus, facere non possit, id profecto est maius et fortius et sapientius homine. homo autem non potest facere caelestia: ergo illud quod haec efficiat uel effecerit, superat hominem arte consilio prudentia potestate.
passages.english: "If there is anything," says Chrysippus, "that accomplishes things which man, although he is endowed with reason, cannot do, that is surely greater and stronger and wiser than man. But man cannot make the heavenly things; therefore that which makes or has made them surpasses man in skill, planning, foresight and power."

passages.original: unus est igitur princeps et origo rerum deus, sicut Plato in Timaeo et sensit et docuit: cuius maiestatem tantam esse declarat, ut nec mente conprehendi nec lingua exprimi possit.
passages.english: There is therefore one God, the first principle and origin of things, as Plato both thought and taught in the Timaeus; and he declares his majesty to be so great that it can neither be grasped by the mind nor expressed by the tongue.

passages.original: idem testatur Hermes, quem Cicero ait in numero deorum apud Aegyptios haberi, eum scilicet qui ob uirtutem multarumque artium scientiam Termaximus nominatus est, et erat non modo Platone, uerum etiam Pythagora septemque illis sapientibus longe antiquior.
passages.english: Hermes bears the same witness, whom Cicero says is counted among the gods by the Egyptians, namely the one who, on account of his excellence and his knowledge of many arts, was named Thrice-Greatest; and he was far more ancient not only than Plato but also than Pythagoras and those seven sages.

passages.original: apud Xenophontem Socrates disputans ait formam dei non oportere conquiri, et Plato in Legum libris, quid omnino sit deus. non esse quaerendum, quia nec inueniri possit nec enarrari.
passages.english: In Xenophon, Socrates, in discussion, says that the form of God ought not to be inquired into; and Plato, in the books of the Laws, [says] that what God is at all should not be sought, because it can neither be found nor fully described.
passages.notes: The punctuation of the edition (a full stop after 'deus') splits the sentence; it is translated as one continuous statement, with 'non esse quaerendum' depending on Plato.

passages.original: Pythagoras quoque unum deum conStetur dicens incorporalem esse mentem quae per omnem rerum naturam diffusa et intenta uitalem sensum cunctis animantibus tribuat. Antisthenes autem in Physico unum esse naturalem deum dixit, quamuis gentes et urbes suos habeant populares deos.
passages.english: Pythagoras too acknowledges one God, saying that he is an incorporeal mind which, spread and extended through the whole nature of things, bestows the sense of life on all living creatures. And Antisthenes in his Physicus said that there is one natural god, although nations and cities have their own popular gods.

passages.original: unde intellegimus religionis ac iustitiae causa esse hominem figuratum. cuius rei testis est Marcus Tullius in libris De legibus ita dicens: sed omnium quae in doctorum hominum disputatione uersantur, nihil est profecto praestabilius quam plane intellegi nos ad iustitiam esse natos.
passages.english: From this we understand that man was formed for the sake of religion and justice. A witness of this is Marcus Tullius in his books On the Laws, speaking thus: "But of all the things that are discussed in the disputations of learned men, nothing is surely more excellent than to understand clearly that we were born for justice."

passages.original: sed occurrit nobis Epicurus ac dicit: \'si est in deo laetitiae adfectus ad gratiam et odii. ad iram, necesse est habeat et timorem et 5 libidinem et cupiditatem ceterosque adfectus, qui sunt inbecillitatis humanae\'.
passages.english: But Epicurus confronts us and says: 'If there is in God an emotion of joy leading to favour, and of hatred leading to anger, he must necessarily also have fear and lust and desire and the other emotions which belong to human weakness.'
passages.notes: The stray numeral '5' is a line number from the printed edition and has been omitted.

passages.original: \'Deus\' inquit Epicurus \'nihil curat\'. nullam igitur habet potestatem — curare enim necesse est eum qui habeatuel si habet et non utitur, quae tanta neglegentiae causa est ut ei non dicam nostrum genus, sed etiam mundus ipse sit uilis ?
passages.english: 'God,' says Epicurus, 'cares for nothing.' Then he has no power, for whoever has [power] must necessarily care. Or if he has it and does not use it, what reason for neglect is so great that, I will not say our race, but even the world itself should be worthless to him?
passages.notes: 'habeatuel' is a scanning error for 'habeat. uel'.

passages.original: nescisse autem philosophos quae ratio esset irae, apparet ex finitionibus eorum quas Seneca enumerauit in libris quos De ira conposuit. ira est inquit cupiditas ulciscendae iniuriae aut ut ait Posidonius, cupiditas puniendi eius a quo te inique putes laesum. quidam ita finierunt: ira est incitatio animi ad nocendum ei qui aut nocuit aut nocere uoluit. Aristotelis definitio non multum a nostra abest.
passages.english: That the philosophers did not know what the nature of anger was is evident from their definitions, which Seneca listed in the books he composed On Anger. "Anger," he says, "is the desire to avenge a wrong," or, as Posidonius says, "the desire to punish the one by whom you think you have been unjustly harmed." Some have defined it thus: "Anger is an arousing of the mind to harm the one who has either harmed or wished to harm." Aristotle's definition is not far from ours.

passages.original: unicum hoc exemplum temperantiae putant, sed auctoritate ducti non uident quam inepta et locutus fuerit et fecerit. nam si, ut ait Plato, nemo prudens punit, quia peccatum est, sedne peccetur, apparet quam malum uir sapiens proposuerit exemplum.
passages.english: They think this a unique example of self-restraint, but, led by [his] authority, they do not see how foolishly he both spoke and acted. For if, as Plato says, no prudent man punishes because a wrong has been done, but so that wrong may not be done, it is clear what a bad example the wise man set.
passages.notes: 'sedne' is read as 'sed ne'. The person whose example is meant is not named in the passage, presumably someone mentioned just before.

passages.original: restat ut more Ciceronis utamur epilogo ad perorandum. sicut ille in Tusculanis de morte disserens fecit, ita nos in hoc opere testimonia diuina quibus credi possit adhibere debemus, ut illorum persuasionem reuincamus qui sine ira deum esse credentes dissoluunt omnem religionem: sine qua, ut ostendimus, aut inmanitate beluis aut stultitia pecudibus adaequamur;
passages.english: It remains for us, after Cicero's manner, to use an epilogue to conclude. As he did in the Tusculans when discussing death, so in this work we ought to bring forward divine testimonies which can be believed, so as to refute the persuasion of those who, believing that God is without anger, destroy all religion. Without it, as we have shown, we are made equal either to wild beasts in savagery or to cattle in stupidity;

passages.original: Apollodorus quidem ut de ciui ac populari sua gloriatur, Fenestella uero etiam legatos Erythras a senatu esse missos refert, ut huius Sibyllae carmina Romam deportarentur et ea consules Curio et Octauius in Capitolio, quod tunc erat curante Quinto Catulo restitutum, ponenda curarent.
passages.english: Apollodorus indeed boasts of her as his fellow citizen and countrywoman, while Fenestella even reports that envoys were sent by the senate to Erythrae so that the verses of this Sibyl might be brought to Rome, and that the consuls Curio and Octavius saw to it that they were placed in the Capitol, which had then been restored under the supervision of Quintus Catulus.

passages.original: Verum quia plures, ut ostendi, Sibyllae a doctissimis auctoribus fuisse traduntur, unius testimonium satis non sit ad confirmandam sicut intendimus ueritatem.
passages.english: But since, as I have shown, there are said by the most learned authors to have been several Sibyls, the testimony of one may not be enough to confirm the truth, as we intend.

passages.original: simili modo deflagrationem postea futuram uaticinata est, qua rursus inpietas hominum deleatur: καί τοτε γινώσκειν θεὸν οὐκέτι πραὺν ἐόντα,ἀλλὰ χόλῳ βρίθοντα καὶ ἐξολέκοντά τε γένναν ἀνθρώπων ἅμα πᾶσαν ὑπ\' ἐμπρησμοῦ μεγάλοιο. unde apud Nasonem de Ioue ita dicitur:
passages.english: In a similar way she prophesied the conflagration to come afterwards, by which the impiety of men will again be destroyed: 'And then [they will] know God no longer gentle, but heavy with wrath and destroying the whole race of men together by a great burning.' Hence in Naso [Ovid] it is said of Jupiter as follows:
passages.notes: In the Greek, 'ἐξολέκοντα' is presumably for 'ἐξολέκοντα'/'ἐξολλύντα' (destroying), and 'γένναν' is for 'γένναν'/'γέννην' (race). The Greek also lacks a space after 'ἐόντα,'. The quotation from Ovid follows outside the passage.
